game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer. All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed. One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead. Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting. In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels. Stay vigilant.

review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If I could describe [i]Orwell[/i] in just two words, it would be "surprisingly smart". By that I mean: this is, obviously, a game about ubiquitous government surveillance, and that's not exactly a new theme. It would have been really easy to slap a "Big Brother BAD" plot on this, make it all about how you're one lone hero fighting the implacable government machine, give it a nice feel-good ending and be done with it. Or go the other way and go full grimdark with the boot stamping on a human face, forever. But [i]Orwell[/i] avoids taking the easy way out, and presents a very human story about how real people might act in a world where such a surveillance system exists. Sure, all the endings you can get (and there's a few) are still much more optimistic than George Orwell would be comfortable with, but hey, if you want [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i], you know where to get it.

The gameplay is a simple affair where, in your role as a government agent, you look through available information (websites, chat transcripts, telephone calls) and collect relevant "data chunks", which in turn unlock more avenues for gathering information... and that's less boring than I'm making it sound, honest. For starters, it's not completely linear: sometimes the data you can collect is contradictory, irrelevant, or just plain wrong when taken out of context, and you have to apply your best judgement as to what goes in -- and the very fact that you're telling the system what to think of people based on the information you select comes back to haunt you in the story. Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game, or something that will challenge you beyond "did I forget to click on something somewhere", this isn't it. You're basically here for the story, but there's enough agency that you don't feel like you might as well have been reading a novel.

[i]Orwell[/i] isn't perfect. I got "stuck" once or twice when the game wanted me to put in some information I had deemed not worth uploading, or that I'd left to come back to later when I had more data -- the interface will track what you have and haven't seen, but not what you've seen but haven't acted upon. At these points (and some others) suspension of disbelief suffers a bit by the way the game artificially fences off information that, logically, should be available at any time. The graphics, while suitably stylized, are a bit [i]too[/i] stylized, especially when things need to animate. The music is fine (with some dramatic touches for when you've uncovered particularly dramatic info), but not remarkable. None of these things are deal breakers, though, and overall [i]Orwell[/i] is well worth its price tag as a solid, interactive story experience with an "It Could Happen Here!" theme that makes it that much more compelling.

review_text_raw:
My son (13 - somewhat advanced for his age) and I played this game together and had a blast. We stayed up until the wee hours of the morning trying to solve the puzzle and figure out who the bad guys were and hopefully, just maybe, make the right choices.

Except, sometimes there seems to be no right choice!

This is basically a super-clever way of telling a story but making you feel like you are in control. In reality there are a couple of ways it can play out, but you are still following a storyline.

In some ways, it is like Bandersnatch for those of you familiar with it.

We had a BLAST playing this and are looking forward to trying out the future installments. Great job doing this and hopefully it will teach a new generation some of the terrors that come along with George Orwell's writings.

If you have never read 1984 and Animal Farm, you owe it to yourself to watch the movies, read the books or find some way to consume them that you enjoy. Like Ayn Rand's Anthem, Atlas Shrugged and Fountainhead, they are important stories to have at least given some thought.

review_text_raw:
I wrote this review after 3 episodes, I might change it later.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

It led to a very aggravating moment where I had to chose between two options, I took the wrong one and innocent people died. To add insult to injury, my sidekick had the nerve to patronize me "What did we do wrong ? If we had taken the other option, this could have been avoided". I think it was meant to emotionally disturb me and make me think that this investigation method is fundamentally flawed, on top of being ethically reprehensible. But instead all I could think was "F*ck you, all informations you ALLOWED me to get pointed at the first option being the good one. You think you're cleverly ambiguous but you're just a cheap mystery novel deliberately misleading the audience to make the plot last long enough".

In conclusion, an extremely lukewarm approval, that might lead to a disapproval if they keep doing this in future episodes. I don't want to replay this game as it feels like Telltale's Walking Dead, where the illusion of choice disappears at the second playthrough where different choices don't impact as much as they seemed.

EDIT : I finished the 5 chapters, I keep my extremely uncommitted approval (lets say 50.1/100).
What limits this game the most is its linearity. I compared it to a mystery novel, it's even worse in late episodes, they want you to suspect specific people in specific orders punctuated by specific twists. You learn in chapter 5 crucial informations that you had no reason not to discover in chapters 1 and 2, since you follow the exact same protocol except the game deliberately kept informations away from you in order to make the game last 5 chapters.

The game also has the nerve to make this railroad look like a social commentary. "You've been chasing the wrong people the entire time, this is the proof that Orwell is unreliable !". Yeah but no, this is just proof that you're putting arbitrary limitations for the sake of the narrative. And even with that, Orwell did better than any other investigation method. Call it unethical, dangerous, tyrannical if you want, but it gets sh*t done and saved lives, and would have done even better without the railroad.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

review_text_raw:
I got this game for free, quite some time ago; But I never gave it the attention it deserves. The topics covered are very current and constantly debated. They generate controversy and distrust towards the authority itself.
Is it right to "spy" on the population in the name of security?
Is it right to authorize criminal actions based only on fragments of information or alleged crimes committed?
Is it right to use AI to track, follow and spy on people?
As you play Orwell, these questions will echo in your mind.
This game is inspired by the novel "1984" by Orwell.
You will find yourself behind a monitor of an advanced surveillance system and you will have to collect information on various people to "avoid" new crimes.
The gameplay is similar to a text adventure, where you have to read the information and decide which ones to load into the system. The interface is very simple and everything is explained very well at the beginning of the game.
The plot is very well developed and will hopefully raise some ethical questions about what you are doing.
This game is a little gem in a niche genre.
It is definitely worth playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is an intriguing game that does not let you get away with bad jokes. The player will have to use rationality and puzzle together the real story from reading other people's perspectives on the same events, and one must be careful what information is handed over to Big Brother.

The game lets you choose whether you want to let people get away with things or if you hand every piece of information to your superior, and it's easy to let yourself be brainwashed and forget that one surveills real people and not just stains in the system, which the game is really good at making you believe. In addition to this, the game had good sound effects which kept you on the edge of your seat, as well as having many plot-twists and unexpected elements to it. 
Not to mention the witty references to the novel 1984 by George Orwell, which effectively added an element of familiarity to those who are acquainted with the novel.

I recommend this game to both people who know 1984 and to those who don't (and possibly want to), as this is a good introduction to the novel and it gives you an interesting perspective in how it feels to work for Big Brother. Therefore, I give this game a rating of 10/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Some people say that the internet and social networks are the worst enemies of dictatorial regimes. But what if that’s not the case?
In Orwell, you will take on the role of an investigator working for the government. 
Your goal is to identify those responsible for a terrorist attack and to do so, you’ll have access to Orwell, a computer system capable of blurring the line between public and private information, allowing you to spy and, if you choose, condemn your suspects.

Primarily, the game involves selecting and collecting datachunks about your targets, which gradually unlock additional sources of information. These may offer useful clues or potentially lead you to an entirely different person. This process continues until at least one incriminating piece of evidence is discovered.

Pros:
[list]
[*]The game’s concept is quite unique
[*]Intuitive gameplay with investigative puzzles
[*]You can change the course of the events with your choices
[/list]


Cons:
[list]
[*]Very short, around 5 hours of gameplay
[*]Low replayability
[/list]

[b]Conclusion[/b]
If you enjoy investigative puzzle games and don’t mind reading walls of text, Orwell is a really interesting title, especially for its themes and ethical implications.
Its main downside is that it doesn’t last long, about 5 hour and the gameplay lacks variety, as most of the game mechanics are introduced within the first 15 minutes of gameplay.
I recommend it especially if it’s on sale.

review_text_raw:
Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 312:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a tense, thought-provoking surveillance thriller that does more with a few browser tabs and text files than most games do with entire cities. It casts you as a government contractor sifting through personal data to uncover a growing threat—and forces you to wrestle with how much “truth” you really need to keep people safe. It’s slick, unsettling, and surprisingly emotional.

[b]🪬 Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Brilliant UI that doubles as storytelling. The whole game takes place inside a simulated desktop, with tabs for social media, chat logs, police records, and more. But it’s not just aesthetic! It feels like doing a job. Every click, every search result, every drag-and-drop data point creates tension. The interface is intuitive, immersive, and sinister.

[*] Deep moral ambiguity in every decision. Do you report that someone once expressed violent thoughts in a song lyric? Do you include their real name in a classified file? What about the context? The game forces you to make hard calls on limited info, and the consequences are immediate. 

[*] Tightly written and emotionally resonant. Despite being mostly text, the characters come alive through their messages, posts, and private calls. You start to see their contradictions, their fears, their humor. It’s intimate in a way that hits hard when you're the one deciding what gets flagged—and what gets buried.

[*] Great balance of investigation and puzzle-solving. The game isn’t about cracking codes or hacking firewalls: it’s about connecting dots. Who knows who? What’s fact, what’s hearsay, and what might get someone arrested? You feel clever when you catch a subtle connection between a dating profile and a news article. It’s simple but deeply satisfying.

[*] Fantastic pacing and structure. The game unfolds over five episodes, each building tension and complexity. Just when you think you know what’s going on, it flips your assumptions. It’s rare to find a game this compact that still manages to feel complete and impactful.
[/list]

👁️ [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Limited replay value. While your choices do have consequences, the story arc mostly funnels toward the same endpoint with slight variations. It’s a brilliant one-time experience, but it may not have the branching depth to support multiple playthroughs.

[*] Some plot twists feel a bit on-the-nose. The writing is mostly subtle, but a few characters and twists lean heavily into dystopian clichés. It's forgivable, especially for a debut game, but occasionally the nuance slips.

[*] A bit short. For players used to longer visual novels or narrative-driven games, [i]Orwell[/i] might feel more like an extended episode than a full series. That said, it’s tightly packed and doesn’t waste your time.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Interactive story hidden behind a simple detective game [/h1]

While the game's premise sounds pretty interesting, the gameplay is quite simple. You read various things such as Internet pages (forums, bank account extract, company's webpage, etc), chat discussions,  listen to live calls which are transcribed and some parts of the text will be highlighted which you can then drag and drop to [b]Orwell[/b], a database which unlocks additional things if a link can be established with the information you've taken.
For a non-spoiler example: you search a person's personal blog and you can find and analyze their username which can then be linked to another forum where it's used for more juicy contents.

It's a bit like [u]A Lost Phone[/u] but its puzzles are MUCH simpler and you can't really get stuck for too long as there's plenty of helpful indicators. Actually, the best part of the game where I really concentrated was when the amount of datachunks (highlighted parts of data in texts) you could import was limited. This really made you think if a [strike]favorite color[/strike] hobby such as artist is a valuable piece of data or not (you could be redirected to an artist page showing past gigs/locations or a contact phone number!).

The best part of the game is the story, because in the end, there's a story and it's told little by little, there are some interesting plot parts (Sorry won't spoil anything) and even if the gameplay sounds boring, the pace is really good and I didn't see time pass by while I finished the 5 episodes. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Smart, subtle, and shockingly good: this one lingers long after the credits.[/h1]

Ever wondered what it would feel like to be Big Brother’s favorite intern? Orwell hands you the surveillance keys to a digital dystopia and asks: how far is too far when safety is on the line? Presented through simulated internet searches, social media sleuthing, and a stripped-down but powerful interface, this game is one of the most immersive narrative experiences I’ve played!

The choices are yours: what do you report? What gets ignored? You might think you're just dragging datachunks into files, but your decisions have real consequences, shaping a gripping narrative with multiple endings and gray-area morality at every turn. It’s as if Papers Please had a love child with 1984 and that baby learned to code.

There is a catch though : this isn't really a “puzzle” game despite the label (it’s more like an interactive spy-thriller/visual novel hybrid with branching paths and big philosophical questions). That said, I devoured it across three playthroughs to 100% the game and would gladly do more. Whether you’re a dystopia enthusiast or just looking for a smart, haunting slow burn, Orwell belongs on your must-play list, especially when it goes on sale (but even at full price, it’s a steal with around 4 hours of game play per playthrough).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is pretty fascinating, and I am looking forward to the next episodes (this is being released in episodes, bit by bit). Basically, you are being "Big Brother", hacking into personal files, browsing social media sites in order to solve and prevent crimes. 

Surely, there is a pretty obvious message here, which might be a bit too moralistic for some, but then again, I find it fascinating how you can actually upload unclear information (which is in conflict with another bit of information) and thereby push the investigation into the wrong direction.

Example: One guy mentions "torture", but didn't mean actual physical torture, but more like "it was torture to wait", more like in a fun way. However, if you pull that term and upload it, you will convince your superiors that the person is actually into torturing other people, thereby painting a totally wrong picture, distorting the facts. 
Which is what actually happens a lot, not only on the web, irl. 

The game has a certain indie, Papers Please type vibe... the focus here is on the storyline and your activities, and I think it's quite fascinating. The devs did well, letting you browse websites, hack into chats, wiretap phones, hacking desktops. Sure, it will eventually feel a bit "on rails", as you basically look for bits marked in blue and upload them, progressing the story with that, and the relevant bits are the only ones you can use and upload... so the game kind of leads you by the hand. All you do is read and scroll, find the info, drag it to the upload queue. 

However... I do think that a) if you bother to read what is going on, it might actually make you think a bit, and b) the story is pretty interesting, and I can't wait to see where all this leads. Really like the periodic release... every week, there is a new episode, which you are being told about by email. 

In a nutshell - this is a rather interesting little game with some very cool ideas. It might make you think about the story, government involvement, whether the end always justifies the means, and you might ponder who is right and who is wrong in this story. 
There are some technical problems (for example, if you play this on two different devices, you might run into a problem with starting the game on one of them), but the devs are looking into any problem and are clearly communicating what is going on - nice job there. 

Bottom-line
Great little game, eager to see more of it. Quite a bit of reading involved, but this game will make you think, it's an interesting take on the whole idea of Big Brother is watching you, and is quite well executed. 

So far: 7.5/10, score will probably go up once more episodes are released

That's why I liked Orwell so much. The creators don't force their point of view on you, but rather make you think about it. There is no black and white - just two sides of the same coin.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If you like to exercise your mind, this is a game for you. If you like to be nosy or adore crime thriller, this is also the game for you. Orwell really teases your brain and forces you to keep track of your steps as you're made to retrace them again and again.

If you don't like milling through data and tasks that require you be VERY thorough and thoughtful, this game is not for you. You will find it boring. Although a lot of fun, I can easily see how one might find this boring. This is truly an NSA simulator--you're rifling thorugh data, and tons of it. If you're not one to hunker down and read through information, you'll either get stuck or choose a wrong path. The game is linear in its structure...some choices can send you down different paths but the idea stays the same. I've only finished one playthrough but it's clear when you can take things down a different path.As with true research, you can waste plenty of time collecting incessant things or even collect incorrect information. Your selections DO effect the story and have consequences, similar to the ones you might evoke in real life. You cannot change them, even immediately afterwards. This game has a lot of replay potential as each chapter can deviate significantly as you fill in the holes.

There were two instances where the game requires you to input 'useless' or 'false' information in order to progress, which threw me off as most of the game revolves around you putting down as much 'accurate' info as possible.

I truly enjoy how thought provoking Orwell is...I'm not easily emotionally swayed by games, but I legitimately recieved goosebumps during one chapter, where the realizations of what this game implies about government and observation truly sank in....of how surveillance can provide extremes pulled from both the good and the bad.

Not a game for everyone, but an excellent, easygoing and extremely thought-provoking game all the same. I like visual novels and puzzles, but I'm picky as I have a short attention span and am a bit of a snob when it comes to the quality of the plot and writing of the story....I am tempted to play it again, just to see where my choices take me. This rarely happens. I just bought the sequel... 7/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's the first time I give a revew on Steam but I feel I had to do it for this game. I bought it this week and started playing yesterday. I stopped at 3 am to go to bed, then continued playing today as I was completely hooked. I did a complete playthrough in 9.5 hours, which is really great for the price. It could take less time, but I really got invested in the story and actually took time to make every decision carefully. 

TL;DR : This game is a masterpiece. Buy it.
I'll try to break down my impressions :

PROS
-AMAZING storyline! It was intricate, well written, complex... I enjoy puzzles & solving enigmas, I'm not new to it... but this game got me wandering in the dark, completely distabilized. And the side stories just adds to it.
-Well written characters! The game is litterally about digging into targetted people's life, going as deep as possible. It could have been so bad, it could have been superficial data made up just for the story. But it was interesting. You have to make choices, decide what information you give up to Orwell and what other info you keep to yourself, and it impacts the story and these people's life. I developped sympathy for some and aversion for others. The characters felt real.
-The ending was great. At that point, I was expecting it, but it was still so satisfying.
-Very intuitive and easy gameplay. Just a tip : don't go too fast. Wait a bit before sending a piece of information, try to make up your own opinion with other infos first.
-Nice art style. It's simple yet beautiful, I really enjoyed it. 
-Nice soundtrack. The music was always appropriate and guided me through the story. 

CONS
-Only one story. I wish there was more enigmas, I wish it wasn't over! Even if I could change the playthrough slightly, it's still the same. I'm eager to play more of this game!
-Some bugs. Was never really detrimental to my gaming experience, but still slightly annoying. I sometimes had trouble dragging the infos to the dropping box, and somtimes there was the alert symbol like I sill had unseen data chunks, which wasn't true, so I would search for missed info that weren't there. 

CONCLUSION
If you're the kind of player to aggressively click your mouse at every dialogue box to skip it as fast as possible, this game is not for you. It's a game for the critical thinkers, for people who like to pause to think and come up with theories. You have to enjoy reading, because that's basically all what you'll do... it's more of a graphic novel than a video game. But it's so delicously done, if you're open to something different and refreshing, don't hesitate any further, buy this game and dive into it. You won't regret it I promise. :)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.
However, Orwell is far better experienced (in my opinion) to just "do" and let the events unfold.

But as I said, if you are anxious about making the wrong call, you might not enjoy this game.
If you are neither scared by that nor by "this-isn't-a-game"-sayers, then you might really enjoy this game. I picked it up at a sale and enjoyed my time with it - hopefully you will too.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that has motivated me to take the time to write a review again, something I have not done in a while.  I'll admit, the title using the name of the author of a favorite book of mine grabbed my attention, and the description of the gameplay was enough to get me to take the plunge during the winter sale.  What followed was several hours spent parsing through the personal data of a group of fictional persons to solve the mystery of a terror attack and to consider the tradeoffs between privacy and security.

Let me start by saying that Orwell is at no point pedantic.  On the very rare occassion a character has been preachy, it was entirley in character for an activist.  This game has you violating privacy in order to achieve a verifiable and practical good; if you are a successful investigator you can literally save lives.  I'd do a diservice to potential players though to say any more than the very vague and cliche question of "At what cost?"

The gameplay is surprisingly interesting and reminded me is a lot of ways of the surprise hit "Papers, Please."  In the not-to-distant future The Party has enacted a new security measure that gathers every scrap of digital information a person could leave.  However, to address internal privacy concerns no one person sees everything and makes decisions.  You play an "Investigator" who has been hired to comb through relevant data as determined by the search algorythims of the Orwell system.  As you read people's emails, chatlogs, and visit their blogs and social media sites you decide what information to pass onto your Advisor.  His role is to determine who merits investigation and draw conclusions from the data you send.  That is to say, the only information the insider in law enforcement is allowed to see is what you deem relevant.  To do your job well you must avoid not only missing relevant data, but oversharing data that could be taken out of context or is irrelevant.  Of course, since it is completley up to you to decide what is relevant, this opens the door to different investigation outcomes I fully intend to explore in future playthroughs, even if I do know the answer to the mystery.

The mystery is also quite enthralling.  I write this review at 3AM, having completed the game in a single sitting of several hours, sucked in by the need to uncover "just one more" piece of the puzzle until suddenly I was furiously not only trying to solve the whole riddle, but making ethical considerations over what I should share or if I should continue to do my job "properly."  If you enjoy a good mystery or if you like very interactive VN-style games like Analogue: A Hate Story (which I also reccomend), then I can't tell you to buy this quickly enough, even if it isn't on sale.  This was a unique and wonderful gaming experience that I am glad I had.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Loosely based on '1984', the critically acclaimed dystopian novel by George Orwell about state surveillance and the horrors that unavoidably come with it, 'Orwell' delivers an immersing story taking five or six hours to complete. You are an investigater looking for information about recent terrorist activities, which will hopefully lead to the arrest of the perpetrators. But information does not necessarily equal facts...

If you are interested in topics like politics, freedom, security, and ethics, this game is well worth your time. Most choices you get to make don't matter that much, it's all in the narrative that is frighteningly close to what is happening right now in most countries in the world; hundreds of thousands of people worldwide evaluating and interpreting the actions of all people in the vicinity of camera's, phone's or computers. This game shows how easy it can be to find these people guilty of something. Anyone.

Nice artwork, great writing and plot twists. Nicely disconcerting music. Interface is sometimes a little clogged (lots of scrolling), but clear and fluid.

Good reads on this topic are 'Little brother' by Cory Doctorow and Philip K Dick's 'Minority report'.

TL;DR the famous quote "Any society that would give up a little liberty to gain a little security, will deserve neither and lose both" by Benjamin Franklin is explained by this game. 9/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
There's a demo that already tells quite a lot about this game. I'll just assume now that you've already played the demo and I will only go into details.

Episode 1 (the demo) is great: You have a target, you dig into her personal information, discover her personality, her social media accounts, her relations. You feel like digging into information you're not supposed to know, you're spying a stranger and soon feel like you know everything about him.

Sadly, Orwell can't keep quality this up. You're still wiretapping calls, crawling through social media accounts, gathering information and finding connections. However, the people aren't really the focus anymore - after episode 1, the story becomes more linear, you'll try to find out information about possible terrorist groups, but the game will just throw all the personal information at you while you're doing that. You don't really have to piece clues together, crawl through articles by yourself or solve riddles.

To summarize, Orwell simply feels like a visual novel that gives you a decision once in a while. Decisions, that - at least that's how they felt to me - barely have any impact. Few datachunks might lead to a different result, most don't, and some have to be uploaded so that the story progresses, even though they might seem misleading to you. However, the game doesn't give you the chance to dig deeper into those datachunks.

In the end, you'll be scrolling through new articles which the game throws at you, extracting 90% of the datachunks you find there to piece together the story while some guy comments every single of your actions. You'll do that for about 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you read the texts, and then the credits will roll.

Don't get me wrong - the story was exciting from beginning to the end, I enjoyed Orwell a lot, but it's way behind its potential. It gives the player almost 0 freedom and one might argue, whether or not this is intentional because of its setting.

If you regret one of your decisions, i.e. you accidentally uploaded a piece of information that you didn't want (which happened to me few times), bad luck. There's only autosave (it saves after every single decision) and you can't replay single chapters - even after finishing the game and can only start from scratch. There's not a lot replayability to it and the achievements are basically "don't upload a specific piece of optional information" which is kind of... meh. But it's the only thing this game offers and I can't imagine it being exciting anymore after you know the story.

If you like the setting, get it for a low price, enjoy it once, never touch it again. Then maybe look at the sequel (Ignorance is Strength) which improves on a few things (it actually gives you some freedom and you have to piece together some clues by yourself), but on the other hand tells a boring cliché story with uninteresting characters that ends after less than 3 hours.

It's so shame because episode 1 was so intriguing, but at least the demo shows you exactly what to expect from this game. If you enjoyed the demo and want more - go for it. If you didn't, skip the game - it won't become better after episode 1.

Few datachunks might lead to a different result, most don't, and some have to be uploaded so that the story progresses, even though they might seem misleading to you. However, the game doesn't give you the chance to dig deeper into those datachunks. In the end, you'll be scrolling through new articles which the game throws at you, extracting 90% of the datachunks you find there to piece together the story while some guy comments every single of your actions. You'll do that for about 3-5 hours, depending on how thoroughly you read the texts, and then the credits will roll. Don't get me wrong - the story was exciting from beginning to the end, I enjoyed Orwell a lot, but it's way behind its potential. It gives the player almost 0 freedom and one might argue, whether or not this is intentional because of its setting. If you regret one of your decisions, i.e. you accidentally uploaded a piece of information that you didn't want (which happened to me few times), bad luck. There's only autosave (it saves after every single decision) and you can't replay single chapters - even after finishing the game and can only start from scratch. There's not a lot replayability to it and the achievements are basically "don't upload a specific piece of optional information" which is kind of... meh. But it's the only thing this game offers and I can't imagine it being exciting anymore after you know the story. If you like the setting, get it for a low price, enjoy it once, never touch it again. Then maybe look at the sequel (Ignorance is Strength) which improves on a few things (it actually gives you some freedom and you have to piece together some clues by yourself), but on the other hand tells a boring cliché story with uninteresting characters that ends after less than 3 hours. It's so shame because episode 1 was so intriguing, but at least the demo shows you exactly what to expect from this game. If you enjoyed the demo and want more - go for it. If you didn't, skip the game - it won't become better after episode 1.

review_text_raw:
TBH, the only reason I finally ended up playing this game over everything else in my backlog was because Gabe Newell said in an interview that he really liked the game.

I liked it too.  I would put the genre closest to this game as a "choose your own adventure" Visual Novel, but without a lot of the VN tropes.

To complete the game is about 5-6 hours. You serve the role as "investigator" and find information on suspects involved in crimes.  Another government official makes arrest decisions based on the information that you choose to (or not to) give him.  You cannot directly communicate with this official, only send him certain pieces of information.

This creates an interesting dynamic. You can present misleading evidence to get people arrested, or you can try to protect those who you think are not troublemakers. You feel like you have a lot of power, but at the same time, you'll often have information misinterpreted. A complaint that I have is that sometimes, certain pieces of information seem completely irrelevant, but are needed to be sent to progress the story. At some points I just found myself essentially uploading everything to make the plot advance.

At certain points in the game you'll be given a choice between 2 conflicting pieces of evidence, where you can only upload one. Sometimes, it was completely unclear which evidence was the "truth". However, other times, I was able to take a logical guess as to what was correct based on other information I had found.

Supposedly, there are multiple endings based on the decisions you make (I have not replayed the game yet). I elected to NOT savescum to get the most desirable outcome (though I think my run was mostly clean), and I highly suggest you don't either. Believe me, it's more !!!FUN!!! that way.

As a whole, it's a very good game with a couple of flaws. Worth buying on a sale. Probably not worth full price unless this type of game interests you.
